summary: The name literally means "the box," and El Cajon sits inside one — a broad, landlocked valley ringed by mountains on nearly every side, which traps heat in summer and produces some of the warmest temperatures in the San Diego metro, often 10–15°F hotter than the coast just 15 miles west. That geography delivers 9.7 hours of average daily sunshine and a 74°F average daytime high, which sounds idyllic until July turns the valley floor into a sustained broiler. With a median home value of $632,800 against a median household income of $66,478, the price-to-income ratio lands near 9.5×, meaning homeownership requires either substantial savings or dual incomes well above the local median; renting at $1,790 per month, meanwhile, consumes roughly 32% of that same median income before taxes. El Cajon functions partly as a bedroom community for San Diego's healthcare, defense, and biotech employers to the west, but it also hosts its own job base along its commercial corridors and in light industry. The downtown strip along Main Street offers a walkable stretch of restaurants, coffee shops, and weekly events, though the surrounding street grid fragments quickly into auto-oriented arterials and highway interchanges — Interstate 8 bisects the city's geography in a way that separates its northern and southern halves. A 20% poverty rate alongside a relatively modest bachelor's-degree attainment of 22.2% points to an economy leaning heavily on service-sector and hourly-wage employment. El Cajon is a place where affordable rents by San Diego County standards and blazing sunshine come packaged with a valley geography that amplifies both the heat and the sense of enclosure.
